The Airport Spur Freeway provides the highway facilities to satisfy these standards. Modified rapid transit service is proposed over the Airport Spur from the terminal to serve both passengers and employees.
3. The environmental statement establishes that the airport spur freeway will provide improved access for residents of the Region to the Region's air carrier airport and also indicates that significant volumes of airport generated vehicular traffic will not be required to travel on surface arterials in the vicinity of the airport. The Airport Spur, providing direct access between the interstate highway system and the new air cargo area being developed as part of the General Mitchell Field Airport Master Plan, will accommodate many ground movements of air cargo, providing additional time savings to shippers using the high speed air cargo services and diverting truck traffic generated by these cargo movements from the local arterial system in the vicinity of the airport.
4. The forecast growth of aviation activities at General Mitchell Field may be updated to generate increased ground travel demands with attendant noise and air pollution regardless of the ground transportation facilities serving the demand. Further, without high service level facilities, time delays attributable to increased ground traffic volumes will adversely affect the total trip involving air and ground travel. The environmental statement indicated that freeway traffic will generate less air pollution than will traffic under a do-nothing alternative over the near term. Both alternatives result in similar air pollution impacts in the long-run when vehicle pollution controls are fully in effect. Although the environmental statement did not specifically evaluate noise levels that might be forecasted for a do-nothing alternative, it did show that noise levels in the Airport Spur corridor would increase on the order of only 2 dBA. The addition to current arterial street noise levels generated by increased travel of airport generated traffic particularly trucks, under a do-nothing alternative could be more unsatisfactory. It can be mentioned that since the proposed Airport Spur is entirely within the 100 Composite Noise Rating Contour associated with aircraft operations using Runway 7R which is already generating unsatisfactory noise conditions, noise levels associated with travel on the Spur will be comparatively insignificant. It thus appears that the Airport Spur, in serving significant airport generated vehicular travel demands, will not only result in less adverse environmental impact than the other alternatives but will also provide the opportunity for improved transit service as an alternative to continued automobile use.
